title: Research field map
purpose: Map a research field so it can be looked at: what the field is made of, who works on it, and where the applied work is.

tool_notes.openalex: works, authors, institutions and concepts in one place, free and without a key — it carries most of the skeleton
tool_notes.crossref: publisher metadata, DOIs and funders, for what OpenAlex has not indexed
tool_notes.arxiv: preprints, which appear here months before anywhere else
tool_notes.a web-search tool: the only way to evidence a company — no free API lists what a private company is working on

kinds.meaning: a work — a paper, a preprint, a trial report. The thing a DOI identifies. Carries doi, and link when it has one
kinds.keywords: paper, article, preprint, study, work, DOI

kinds.meaning: a person who does the work
a subject, question or mechanism the field is about
a working group, usually inside an institution
a university, hospital or public body
a company, and what it is building

kind_notes.one word per thing: `publication` covers papers, preprints and trial reports — a kind is what a node IS, and the everyday words are keywords, not kinds. A graph may still split them (kind `preprint`) if it needs to; every kind renders, and a kind this app has never heard of gets its own colour.
kind_notes.older names: graphs built before this vocabulary may say `scientist` and `concept`; they render exactly the same way, with hash-derived colours. Nothing has to be migrated.

edges.label: authored
edges.meaning: the main link of a research field. --time the year
edges.name: authored

edges.label: targets
edges.meaning: what a company's work addresses, --dir in

edges.label: cites
edges.meaning: the citation skeleton: --from the citing work, --to the cited one, --dir in. Add --style arrow when the map is meant to be read as a citation graph, and `visuals --arrows on` to do it for every directed relation in the graph at once
edges.name: cites

edges.label: co-cited in N works
edges.meaning: two works cited together. Weak by nature, and it should *look* weak: --power 0.05 --style dashed --set cocited=N. The count is data (shown in the panel), the dash is the reading (a broken line nobody mistakes for structure)

edges.label: collaborates on <subject>
edges.meaning: two organisations on the same subject — this makes a cluster legible instead of a fan of lines into one dot

edges.label: co-cited
edges.name: co-cited
edges.meaning: two works cited together by a third. A weaker, temporal signal than a citation: it says the field put them in the same sentence, not that one built on the other. It moves as the literature grows, so it never drives the layout or a claim on its own.

alternative.a work as an edge: a graph that prefers it may keep putting the work in the edge label (researcher → subject, label = the title, --time the year) instead of promoting it to a `publication` node. Both render; the node form carries a doi and can be co-cited, which the edge form cannot.

visuals.node weight: `weight` on a node is what it is worth on this map, and how it was measured is stated once for the whole graph in `meta.weight.metric` — "relevant papers", "thousands of citations (OpenAlex)". Every panel says which of the two a node's number came from: the document, or the graph's own connections. Change the metric and the sizes change; nothing else has to.
visuals.node size: with no `weight` and no `size`, a node is drawn from ½ × the summed power of its edges × a multiplier for its kind — publication 0.1, researcher 1, lab/institution/company 3, subject 10 — so a map is readable before anyone tunes it. Both halves are the graph's to change: `meta.weight.kind_multipliers`, or `weigh --mul subject=20`. `--set size=6` sets a node's weight by hand in the same units.
visuals.edge power: `power` is an edge's strength, where **1 is a normal relation**: `--set power=0.05` on a co-citation says it is texture, not structure, and it is drawn as a hairline at half opacity. A measured number is a different thing — `--set cocited=66` shows 66 in the panel and leaves the line as thin as it should be.
visuals.direction: `dir: in` puts an arrowhead at the `to` end, so a citation or a target reads as pointing at what it acts on.
visuals.level: a node's position on the third axis (foundational low, abstract high). The 3D view is the only place it moves anything; a 2D map laid out by rings or by force ignores it.
visuals.placement: `ring` puts a node on a concentric ring — 0 is the centre, higher numbers are further out — and `x`,`y` put it exactly where it is told. A graph with a ring on any node is laid out as rings; a graph where every node has `x`,`y` is used as given; otherwise the viewer lays it out itself.
visuals.default rings: organisations 0, researchers 1, publications 2, subjects 3 — which is the ask 'companies in the centre, researchers in the middle, subjects on the periphery' expressed as data.
visuals.following a graph: the panel lists a node's connections with the power and properties of each relation, strongest first. Clicking one opens that node and puts it in the middle of the view, so a graph can be walked rather than only looked at.
visuals.what the panel and canvas do together: pointing at a relation in the panel highlights that line on the canvas (including dashed ones, which are drawn on the overlay); the connections block folds by relation word, and a group can be collapsed into its endpoint node, which then wears a ring sized by the mass it hides. What is hidden is always countable from the screen — a collapsed map that does not say what it hides is a lie about the map.

layout.note: Companies and institutions at the centre, researchers in the middle, subjects on the periphery. With authored x,y the viewer uses them as given; with `ring` it builds the rings; with neither it lays the graph out itself.

edge_appearance.style: space-separated words: the stroke and/or the shape. Strokes: `solid`, `dashed`, `dotted`. Shapes: `arrow`, `double`, `clamped`, `rectangle`, `triangle`. So `--style "dotted arrow"` is valid and reads the way somebody would say it. An unknown word is refused by the engine rather than stored, because a style the renderer ignores is a silent loss of meaning.
edge_appearance.color: `--color '#8fa3c8'` — this relation's own colour. A graph can say 'those edges are blue and dotted' and be obeyed; colours are also what make two relations of the same pair distinguishable in the panel.
edge_appearance.dash: `--dash "6 4"` — an explicit pattern, for when solid/dashed/dotted is not the one you mean. Dashes are drawn on a 2D layer over the WebGL canvas (sigma's programs cannot dash), so they cost nothing to add and are drawn in any pattern or colour.
edge_appearance.width: `--width 2` — an explicit line width in px, when `power` is not the right control.
edge_appearance.arrows off by default: a directed relation (`dir: in`) is drawn as a plain line unless the graph asks for heads: `visuals --arrows on` for the whole graph, or `--style arrow` on one edge. A citation map usually wants them; a field map usually does not.
edge_appearance.where it is decided: per edge in the document, and per graph in `meta.visuals` (arrows, edge_width, node_scale, halo). The app has defaults; a document overrides them. Nothing about appearance needs a code change.

notes.what they are: the long form of a node's description, one markdown file per node (or for the subject as a whole), in a `docs/` folder beside the graph document. They are the half of a survey a graph cannot carry: what a thing is, why it matters here, and where the claim comes from.
notes.how to write one: `kg.py note --graph <id> --node <node>` creates `docs/<slug>.md` from a skeleton and points the node at it; `note --graph <id>` does the same for the subject's overview note, which is the draft of whatever is being written about this map.
notes.how they are read: they are inlined into the rendered page (a file opened from `file://` cannot fetch its neighbours) and appear in a second panel, opened from a node's 'read the note' button or the header's 'notes' button.
notes.how they are written back: the panel edits a copy and can download or copy it; the page cannot write to the reader's disk from `file://`. The file's owner is the agent (or the person) working in the folder — which is also why every note is plain markdown in a predictable place.
notes.why they are not optional for bodies: a `subject`/`lab`/`institution`/`company` node must carry at least one sentence from the moment it is created (`add-node` refuses without it), and `review` lists the bodies whose sentence predates the connections around them, because a description of a concept is a claim about a field and the field keeps moving.

scale.the budget: how many nodes a host can actually draw is measured in the browser, not claimed in the file: a graph over ~600 nodes is revealed in growing steps while frame times are watched, and the count that held 30fps becomes the budget for that host. `kg.py capacity --nodes N` can record one for a machine that cannot measure itself.
scale.what happens past it: nothing is deleted and nothing is refused: the viewer collapses the smallest, weakest clusters (per concept) until it fits, draws a ring around each node that has nodes hidden inside it — thicker with the mass hidden — and says in a banner how many nodes are collapsed, with a button to expand anyway.
scale.why not in the file: a node budget is a fact about a machine. The document travels between machines that are not equally fast, so the number is stored per host (browser storage) and only the *fallback* lives in the document.
scale.10k articles: the graph format does not care: nodes and edges are arrays. What it costs is the source, not the store — a 10k-work OpenAlex pull is roughly 10k credits (~$1 on the metered plan) per refresh, and other providers (Crossref, arXiv, PubMed, Semantic Scholar, CORE, DOAJ) cover parts of the same ground for free or nearly. See the skill's `references/providers.md` for who provides what.
